## 2\. Related Work

We review three strands of related work: (1) the evolution of transactional management, particularly the Saga pattern; (2) cognitive limitations of LLMs motivating the need for transactional integrity, independent validation, and context preservation; and (3) multi-agent LLM frameworks and recent attempts to integrate transactional safeguards.

### 2.1. Transaction Management Systems

Transactional models have evolved significantly since Gray introduced the ACID properties (Gray, [1981](https://arxiv.org/html/2503.11951v3#bib.bib21)). In distributed settings, strict ACID guarantees became impractical, prompting models such as BASE (Pritchett, [2008](https://arxiv.org/html/2503.11951v3#bib.bib36)) and long-lived transaction patterns.

The Saga pattern by Garcia-Molina and Salem (Garcia-Molina and Salem, [1987](https://arxiv.org/html/2503.11951v3#bib.bib18)) decomposes long-lived transactions into smaller, locally atomic sub-transactions with compensating steps for failure recovery. This has influenced modern microservice architectures and workflow engines (Richardson, [2018](https://arxiv.org/html/2503.11951v3#bib.bib37)).

Systems such as YAWL (van der Aalst and ter Hofstede, [2005](https://arxiv.org/html/2503.11951v3#bib.bib39)), AWS Step Functions (aws, [2023](https://arxiv.org/html/2503.11951v3#bib.bib1)), and Azure Logic Apps (azu, [2023](https://arxiv.org/html/2503.11951v3#bib.bib2)) embed Saga-style workflows but remain rigid and manually defined, lacking dynamic adaptability. These foundational principles inform 𝖲𝖺𝗀𝖺𝖫𝖫𝖬𝖲𝖺𝗀𝖺𝖫𝖫𝖬\\mathsf{SagaLLM}sansserif\_SagaLLM’s adaptive, LLM-driven extensions.

### 2.2. LLM Limitations Necessitating SagaLLM’s Key Requirements

To realize this complementary relationship between AI and workflow systems, we must first address the specific limitations that prevent current LLMs from functioning effectively in transactional workflows. Our analysis reveals three fundamental limitations that directly motivate 𝖲𝖺𝗀𝖺𝖫𝖫𝖬𝖲𝖺𝗀𝖺𝖫𝖫𝖬\\mathsf{SagaLLM}sansserif\_SagaLLM’s core requirements: transactional integrity, independent validation, and strategic context preservation.

##### Self-Validation Gap Necessitating Independent Validation

LLMs inherently lack robust self-validation mechanisms, a limitation originating from intrinsic boundaries identified by Gödel’s incompleteness theorems, demonstrating fundamental constraints on a system’s ability to verify its own reasoning (Gödel, [1967](https://arxiv.org/html/2503.11951v3#bib.bib22); Chang and Geng, [2025](https://arxiv.org/html/2503.11951v3#bib.bib11)). Recent research confirms that self-refinement techniques (Madaan and Yazdanbakhsh, [2022](https://arxiv.org/html/2503.11951v3#bib.bib33); Li et al., [2023b](https://arxiv.org/html/2503.11951v3#bib.bib30); Jiang et al., [2024](https://arxiv.org/html/2503.11951v3#bib.bib26)), while iterative and beneficial, are unable to surpass inherent capability ceilings to reliably correct deeper logical errors (Huang et al., [2024](https://arxiv.org/html/2503.11951v3#bib.bib24)). In transactional scenarios, these validation gaps manifest as factual inconsistencies, invalid operations, and unreliable plan feasibility assessments (Yamin et al., [2024](https://arxiv.org/html/2503.11951v3#bib.bib47)). Thus, 𝖲𝖺𝗀𝖺𝖫𝖫𝖬𝖲𝖺𝗀𝖺𝖫𝖫𝖬\\mathsf{SagaLLM}sansserif\_SagaLLM incorporates an independent validation framework to mitigate these inherent limitations.

##### Statelessness Necessitating Transactional Integrity

LLMs process each interaction independently, lacking native mechanisms to maintain the state across sequential interactions. This fundamental statelessness necessitates explicit transactional integrity management to maintain coherent operation sequences and ensure robust failure recovery. Without systematic transaction management, LLM-based systems risk state inconsistency, operation losses, and incoherent recovery procedures.

##### Context Limitations and Strategic Preservation

LLMs rely on self-attention mechanisms that prioritize recent tokens, leading to significant degradation in context retention over long sequences. Empirical studies reveal sharp drops in recall beyond token limits (Xiao et al., [2024](https://arxiv.org/html/2503.11951v3#bib.bib46); Modarressi et al., [2025](https://arxiv.org/html/2503.11951v3#bib.bib34)), especially for mid-context information (Liu et al., [2024b](https://arxiv.org/html/2503.11951v3#bib.bib32); Hsieh et al., [2024](https://arxiv.org/html/2503.11951v3#bib.bib23)). Chain-of-thought heuristics (Cemri et al., [2025](https://arxiv.org/html/2503.11951v3#bib.bib5)) further exacerbate this by lacking mechanisms to manage or pass context reliably across steps. These limitations hinder multi-step reasoning (Wei et al., [2022](https://arxiv.org/html/2503.11951v3#bib.bib42); Stechly et al., [2024](https://arxiv.org/html/2503.11951v3#bib.bib38)), as earlier outputs are frequently lost. 𝖲𝖺𝗀𝖺𝖫𝖫𝖬𝖲𝖺𝗀𝖺𝖫𝖫𝖬\\mathsf{SagaLLM}sansserif\_SagaLLM addresses this by explicitly preserving vulnerable context elements—goals, justifications, and dependencies—through structured memory and persistent tracking.

Collectively, these limitations provide strong motivation to address all three key requirements within 𝖲𝖺𝗀𝖺𝖫𝖫𝖬𝖲𝖺𝗀𝖺𝖫𝖫𝖬\\mathsf{SagaLLM}sansserif\_SagaLLM. Comprehensive transaction management, independent validation, and strategic context preservation are essential for reliably deploying LLM-based multi-agent systems (MAS) in critical real-world applications.

### 2.3. Multi-Agent LLM Frameworks and Transaction Limitations

Frameworks such as AutoGen (Wu et al., [2024](https://arxiv.org/html/2503.11951v3#bib.bib45)), LangGraph (LangChain AI, [2024](https://arxiv.org/html/2503.11951v3#bib.bib27)), and CAMEL (Li et al., [2023a](https://arxiv.org/html/2503.11951v3#bib.bib29)) advance multi-agent LLM coordination but fall short in addressing 𝖲𝖺𝗀𝖺𝖫𝖫𝖬𝖲𝖺𝗀𝖺𝖫𝖫𝖬\\mathsf{SagaLLM}sansserif\_SagaLLM’s three core requirements: transactional integrity, independent validation, and context preservation.

##### Missing Transaction Semantics

LangGraph and AutoGen enable structured workflows and agent interactions, but lack built-in atomicity guarantees, compensation logic, or robust failure recovery. AgentScope (Gao et al., [2024](https://arxiv.org/html/2503.11951v3#bib.bib17)) and AFlow (Zhang et al., [2024](https://arxiv.org/html/2503.11951v3#bib.bib49)) introduce limited rollback mechanisms, but do not generalize across workflows.

##### Validation Gaps

Most frameworks are based on LLM self-validation, exposing them to reasoning errors and hallucinations. Systems such as PLASMA (Brahman et al., [2024](https://arxiv.org/html/2503.11951v3#bib.bib4)) improve reliability but omit transaction-level rollback. LLM-MCTS (Zhao et al., [2023](https://arxiv.org/html/2503.11951v3#bib.bib51)) and Tree-of-Thought (Yao et al., [2024](https://arxiv.org/html/2503.11951v3#bib.bib48)) emphasize pre-execution reasoning without runtime consistency checks.

##### Limited Context Preservation

CAMEL preserves dialogue history but lacks mechanisms for tracking state transitions, inter-agent dependencies, or compensatory paths. Broader planning systems (Wei et al., [2025](https://arxiv.org/html/2503.11951v3#bib.bib41)) do not offer persistent context retention strategies.  
  
Unlike these systems, 𝖲𝖺𝗀𝖺𝖫𝖫𝖬𝖲𝖺𝗀𝖺𝖫𝖫𝖬\\mathsf{SagaLLM}sansserif\_SagaLLM treats compensation, validation, and context tracking as first-class design goals—ensuring reliable, recoverable, and intelligent coordination across complex multi-agent workflows.

2.  2.

These mechanisms evaluate agent outputs and inter-agent inputs against constraints, schemas, and dependency graphs. Persistent validation histories are maintained to support rollback triggers and guard against hallucinations or invalid commitments.
    
3.  3.
    
    Context Management: Maintains essential state and dependency information across long-horizon workflows. Rather than relying on ephemeral context windows, 𝖲𝖺𝗀𝖺𝖫𝖫𝖬𝖲𝖺𝗀𝖺𝖫𝖫𝖬\\mathsf{SagaLLM}sansserif\_SagaLLM persistently stores goals, justifications, and compensation plans in structured memory, enabling agents to reason over consistent histories and perform accurate recovery after failures.

### 3.2. Independent Validation Requirements

To address the inherent limitations of LLM self-verification, SAGA introduces a two-tier validation architecture governed by a global validation agent. This agent operates independently of task agents and has visibility into the full transaction history, agent communications, and global state.

##### Intra-Agent Output Validation

The global validation agent inspects the outputs of the individual task agents before those outputs are committed or transmitted. Outputs are checked for:

*   \-
    
    Syntactic correctness (format, schema)
    
*   \-
    
    Semantic coherence and reasoning soundness
    
*   \-
    
    Factual accuracy against context
    
*   \-
    
    Constraint adherence and invariants
    
*   \-
    
    Context preservation and dependency awareness
    

Failures trigger compensations or corrective augmentation.

##### Inter-Agent Input and Dependency Validation

Inputs and messages between agents are validated before delivery. Checks include:

*   \-
    
    Contract conformance
    
*   \-
    
    Dependency satisfaction
    
*   \-
    
    Cross-agent consistency
    
*   \-
    
    Temporal ordering
    
*   \-
    
    Mutual agreement on shared state
    
*   \-
    
    Transaction coherence
    

Failed validations block delivery and invoke recovery.

##### Validation Response Protocols

SAGA defines structured validation outcomes:

*   \-
    
    Rejection: Discard and compensate
    
*   \-
    
    Augmentation: Enhance with clarifications
    
*   \-
    
    Feedback: Record for future adaptation

# Deep Research: ESAA, ESAA-Security, and SagaLLM

Sources reviewed:

1. [arXiv:2603.06365 — ESAA-Security](https://arxiv.org/pdf/2603.06365)  
2. [arXiv:2602.23193 — ESAA](https://arxiv.org/pdf/2602.23193)  
3. [arXiv:2503.11951 — SagaLLM](https://arxiv.org/pdf/2503.11951)

## Executive Synthesis

These three papers are about the same underlying problem:

> LLM agents are probabilistic, context-limited, and weak at self-verification, but real software/security workflows require deterministic state, auditability, rollback, and reproducible evidence.

They converge on a shared architectural answer:

> Do **not** let the LLM be the system of record.  
> Let the LLM emit structured intentions, and place deterministic governance around execution, validation, state mutation, replay, and recovery.

The papers differ mainly in **which governance primitive** they emphasize:

| Paper | Core Primitive | Domain | Main Contribution |
|---|---:|---|---|
| **SagaLLM** | Saga transactions + compensation | Multi-agent planning | Adds rollback, dependency tracking, validation agents, and persistent memory to LLM workflows |
| **ESAA** | Event sourcing + CQRS | LLM-based software engineering | Treats agent work as immutable events; repository state is projected and replay-verified |
| **ESAA-Security** | ESAA specialized for audits | AI-generated code security review | Turns security auditing into a structured, replayable, evidence-based pipeline |

In plain terms:

- **SagaLLM** says: “LLM workflows need transaction recovery.”
- **ESAA** says: “LLM software engineering needs immutable event history.”
- **ESAA-Security** says: “LLM security audits need event-sourced evidence, not free-form security prose.”

---

# 1. Paper-by-Paper Analysis

## 1.1 SagaLLM: Transaction Guarantees for Multi-Agent LLM Planning

**Paper:** [SagaLLM: Context Management, Validation, and Transaction Guarantees for Multi-Agent LLM Planning](https://arxiv.org/abs/2503.11951)  
**Authors:** Edward Y. Chang, Longling Geng  
**Version reviewed:** v3, July 2025

### Core Problem

SagaLLM targets four failures in multi-agent LLM workflows:

1. **Unreliable self-validation**
2. **Context loss**
3. **No rollback / compensation**
4. **Weak inter-agent coordination**

The paper argues that existing systems such as AutoGen, LangGraph, and CAMEL coordinate agents but do not provide strong transactional semantics.

### Architecture

SagaLLM introduces three integrated frameworks:

```mermaid
graph LR
    A[Application Layer] --> B[SagaLLM]
    B --> C[Context Management]
    B --> D[Validation Framework]
    B --> E[Transaction Framework]
    C --> F[LLM Agents]
    D --> F
    E --> F
```

Key components:

- **Saga Coordinator Agent**
- **Global Validation Agent**
- **Transaction Manager**
- **Compensation Manager**
- **Dependency Tracker**
- **Context Manager**

Each workflow step is treated as a transaction:

$$
T_1, T_2, ..., T_n
$$

Each transaction has a compensation:

$$
C_1, C_2, ..., C_n
$$

If transaction $$T_j$$ fails, compensation runs backward:

$$
C_j, C_{j-1}, ..., C_1
$$

### Example Domain

The main example is travel planning:

- Book flight
- Book hotel
- Book train
- Book return flight
- Validate budget, timing, and dependencies
- If one step fails, compensate dependent bookings

### Strengths

- Strong conceptual fit for **multi-step, externally consequential workflows**
- Good use of classical distributed-systems ideas
- Emphasizes independent validation instead of relying on the same LLM to self-correct
- Explicitly models context, dependency, and rollback state

### Weaknesses / Open Questions

- Some claims are broad relative to the experimental evidence shown.
- The artifact URL in the paper appears placeholder-like in the PDF metadata.
- “GlobalValidationAgent” may itself be LLM-based, which raises a recursive trust issue unless paired with deterministic validation.
- Compensation logic is often domain-specific and may be hard to generate safely in production.

### Best Use Case

SagaLLM is strongest for workflows where actions are:

- Long-running
- Interdependent
- Partially reversible
- Externally consequential

Examples:

- Travel booking
- Procurement
- Healthcare workflow orchestration
- Customer support resolution pipelines
- Multi-step business automations

---

## 1.2 ESAA: Event Sourcing for Autonomous Agents

**Paper:** [ESAA: Event Sourcing for Autonomous Agents in LLM-Based Software Engineering](https://arxiv.org/abs/2602.23193)  
**Author:** Elzo Brito dos Santos Filho  
**Submitted:** February 2026

### Core Problem

ESAA argues that agentic coding has a governance gap:

> Agents can plan and modify code, but they lack durable native state, deterministic replay, and forensic traceability.

Instead of treating the repository snapshot as truth, ESAA treats the **event log** as truth.

### Core Architecture

```mermaid
graph LR
    A[LLM Agent] -->|structured intention| B[Orchestrator]
    B --> C[Schema Validation]
    B --> D[Boundary Contracts]
    C --> E[Append-only Event Log]
    D --> E
    E --> F[Projected Roadmap]
    F --> G[Replay Verification]
```

The LLM does not directly mutate state. It emits structured outputs such as:

- `agent.result`
- `issue.report`

The orchestrator then:

1. Validates JSON schema
2. Checks boundary contracts
3. Appends accepted events
4. Applies file-writing effects
5. Reprojects `roadmap.json`
6. Verifies replay/hash consistency

### Canonical Artifacts

The ESAA system uses artifacts such as:

- `.roadmap/activity.jsonl` — append-only event store
- `.roadmap/roadmap.json` — projected read model
- `AGENT_CONTRACT.yaml`
- `ORCHESTRATOR_CONTRACT.yaml`
- `PARCER_PROFILE.*.yaml`

### Main Invariants

The most important governance rules are:

- Agents emit intentions, not direct writes.
- The orchestrator owns mutation.
- Completed tasks are immutable.
- Corrections happen through new issue/hotfix flows.
- State must be replayable from the event log.
- Projection hash must match replayed state.

### Case Studies

The paper reports two validations:

| Case | Scale | Events | Agents | Result |
|---|---:|---:|---:|---|
| Landing page | 9 tasks | 49 events | 3-agent composition | `verify_status=ok` |
| Clinical dashboard | 50 tasks | 86 events | 4 concurrent agents | partial run, `verify_status=ok` |

The second case is more important: it demonstrates multi-agent concurrency, phase gating, and event serialization.

### Strengths

- Very strong governance model for agentic software work
- Clear separation between cognition and mutation
- Event sourcing is a mature and appropriate pattern
- Replay verification is a meaningful trust primitive
- Good fit for auditability, rollback, and forensic reconstruction

### Weaknesses / Open Questions

- The validation is still small-scale.
- `verify_status=ok` proves replay consistency, not necessarily software quality.
- It needs stronger evaluation against real-world benchmarks or production repositories.
- Conflict resolution is acknowledged as future work.
- The paper would benefit from clearer comparison against LangGraph-style durable state plus checkpointing.

### Best Use Case

ESAA is strongest for:

- Agentic software development
- Multi-agent coding pipelines
- Regulated code generation
- High-accountability AI-assisted engineering
- Systems where “what changed, why, by whom, and when” matters

---

## 1.3 ESAA-Security: Event-Sourced Security Audits

**Paper:** [ESAA-Security: An Event-Sourced, Verifiable Architecture for Agent-Assisted Security Audits of AI-Generated Code](https://arxiv.org/abs/2603.06365)  
**Author:** Elzo Brito dos Santos Filho  
**Submitted:** March 2026

### Core Problem

ESAA-Security applies ESAA to a specific high-value domain:

> AI-generated code may appear functional but remain structurally insecure.

The paper criticizes prompt-based security review because it often has:

- Uneven coverage
- Weak reproducibility
- Unsupported findings
- No immutable audit trail
- Inconsistent severity assignment
- Poor linkage from evidence to final report

### Core Contribution

ESAA-Security reframes security auditing as a governed evidence pipeline.

It defines:

- **4 phases**
- **26 tasks**
- **16 security domains**
- **95 executable checks**

### Audit Pipeline

```mermaid
graph LR
    A[Reconnaissance] --> B[Domain Audit Execution]
    B --> C[Risk Classification]
    C --> D[Final Reporting]
```

### Security Domains

The paper mentions domains including:

- Secrets and configuration
- Authentication
- Authorization
- Input validation
- Dependency and supply chain
- API security
- File upload
- Cryptography
- AI/LLM security
- DevSecOps

### Output Artifacts

The framework produces:

- Structured check results
- Vulnerability inventories
- Severity classifications
- CIA impact reasoning
- Risk matrices
- Technical remediations
- Best-practice guidance
- Executive summaries
- Final Markdown and JSON reports

### Key Architectural Shift

In a normal LLM audit:

> The model’s prose becomes the audit.

In ESAA-Security:

> The final report is only a projection of admitted, structured, replay-verifiable audit events.

That is the most important idea in the paper.

### Strengths

- Strong alignment with real security audit needs
- Good fit for OWASP Top 10 / ASVS-style evidence gathering
- Explicitly separates evidence, classification, remediation, and executive summary
- Better than “ask an LLM to review this repo”
- Especially relevant for AI-generated or “vibe-coded” software

### Weaknesses / Open Questions

- This is more of an architecture/proposal than an empirical benchmark paper.
- The paper defines an evaluation plan but does not yet provide strong comparative results.
- Quality depends heavily on playbook/check quality.
- Replayability does not guarantee vulnerability completeness.
- It does not replace penetration testing, dynamic analysis, or human security expertise.

### Best Use Case

ESAA-Security is strongest for:

- Internal security review of AI-generated code
- Repeatable AppSec audits
- Pre-release hardening
- Evidence-backed security reporting
- Regulated environments needing audit trails

---

# 2. Cross-Paper Architectural Comparison

## Shared Design Philosophy

All three papers reject “LLM as sovereign executor.”

They instead propose:

```mermaid
graph TD
    A[LLM Reasoning] --> B[Structured Intent]
    B --> C[Validation Layer]
    C --> D[Deterministic Orchestrator]
    D --> E[Durable State]
    E --> F[Replay / Recovery / Audit]
```

The LLM is useful for:

- Reasoning
- Planning
- Drafting
- Classification
- Proposing actions

But the system needs deterministic machinery for:

- Validation
- State transition
- Logging
- Recovery
- Replay
- Audit

## Key Difference: Event Sourcing vs Saga Transactions

| Dimension | SagaLLM | ESAA / ESAA-Security |
|---|---|---|
| Main model | Saga transaction | Event sourcing |
| Failure handling | Compensation / rollback | Issue or hotfix path; replay verification |
| State source of truth | Persistent transaction state | Append-only event log |
| Best for | Business workflows with reversible steps | Software engineering and audit trails |
| Validation | Global validation agent | Schema + contracts + orchestrator |
| Recovery model | Compensate failed transactions | Rebuild projection, preserve immutable history |

They are complementary, not competing.

A mature agent platform may need both:

- **Event sourcing** for immutable audit history
- **Saga compensation** for reversible external actions

---

# 3. Critical Takeaways

## 3.1 The strongest idea across all papers

The most important shared insight is:

> Agent reliability should be achieved through architecture, not prompting alone.

Better prompts help, but they do not solve:

- State drift
- Missing evidence
- Context degradation
- Unauthorized effects
- Poor rollback
- Weak auditability
- Non-reproducible conclusions

These papers push toward **agent governance kernels**.

## 3.2 The biggest unresolved issue

The unresolved question is not whether these architectures are sensible. They are.

The harder question is:

> How much substantive task quality do they improve, beyond improving traceability?

For example:

- ESAA can prove that the roadmap projection is replayable.
- ESAA-Security can prove that findings flowed through structured audit events.
- SagaLLM can show that compensation paths exist.

But none of that automatically proves:

- The code is good.
- The security findings are complete.
- The compensation logic is correct.
- The global validation agent is trustworthy.
- The workflow outcome is optimal.

So the architecture improves **governance quality**, but more evidence is needed for **domain quality**.

## 3.3 The main practical risk

The main practical risk is building a beautifully governed system around weak playbooks or weak validators.

In other words:

> A bad audit can be perfectly replayable.

Governance does not replace domain expertise. It amplifies and preserves it.

---

# 4. How This Maps to the Three-Layer Audit Pattern

Your preferred audit methodology — **Architecture → UX → Live QA** — maps very naturally onto these papers.

## Layer 1: Architecture

Questions:

- Is there deterministic orchestration?
- Are agent outputs constrained?
- Is there an append-only log?
- Are state projections reproducible?
- Are task boundaries explicit?
- Is there a rollback or hotfix mechanism?

Relevant paper:

- ESAA
- SagaLLM

## Layer 2: UX / Operator Experience

Questions:

- Can a human understand what happened?
- Are findings traceable?
- Are reports actionable?
- Are errors recoverable?
- Are risk priorities clear?
- Does the workflow reduce cognitive load?

Relevant paper:

- ESAA-Security
- SagaLLM

## Layer 3: Live QA

Questions:

- Can the system run end-to-end?
- Can it recover from failed or invalid outputs?
- Does replay verification pass?
- Are compensations tested?
- Are security findings grounded in evidence?
- Does the final report match the underlying artifacts?

Relevant paper:

- All three

A robust agent audit framework should therefore evaluate both:

1. **Governance correctness**
2. **Outcome correctness**

---

# 5. Recommended Combined Architecture

The best synthesis would combine all three:

```mermaid
graph TD
    A[User Goal / Audit Scope] --> B[Roadmap / Workflow Compiler]
    B --> C[Task Agents]
    C --> D[Structured Intentions]
    D --> E[Schema + Contract Validation]
    E --> F[Event Store]
    F --> G[Projected State]
    G --> H[Replay Verification]

    E --> I[Saga Coordinator]
    I --> J[Compensation Registry]
    J --> K[Rollback / Recovery]

    G --> L[Evidence Artifacts]
    L --> M[Risk Classification]
    M --> N[Final Report]
```

This gives you:

- ESAA’s event log
- SagaLLM’s compensation model
- ESAA-Security’s audit/reporting pipeline

For real-world agentic systems, this is the right direction.

---

# 6. Final Assessment

## Overall Ranking by Maturity

| Rank | Paper | Maturity | Why |
|---:|---|---|---|
| 1 | **ESAA** | Highest architectural concreteness | Includes artifacts, contracts, event vocabulary, schemas, case studies |
| 2 | **SagaLLM** | Strong conceptual system | Good transactional model, but validation and artifacts need scrutiny |
| 3 | **ESAA-Security** | Strong domain specialization | Valuable framework, but more empirical validation needed |

## Bottom Line

These papers are highly aligned and mutually reinforcing.

The strongest conclusion is:

> The future of reliable agent systems is not just better models. It is **evented, validated, replayable, compensable orchestration** around models.

For security audits specifically, ESAA-Security’s most valuable contribution is its insistence that an AI audit should be:

- Explicit in scope
- Structured in evidence
- Reproducible by replay
- Traceable from check to final report
- Useful for remediation, not just vulnerability narration

That is a strong architectural direction — especially for AI-generated codebases.

Understood — I’ll use the **Architecture → UX → Live QA** pipeline.

For these three papers, the pipeline should be:

```mermaid
graph LR
    A[Architecture Audit] --> B[UX / Operator Audit]
    B --> C[Live QA / Validation Audit]
    C --> D[Actionable Findings]
```

## 1. Architecture Audit

Evaluate whether the system has the right governance primitives.

### Checks

- Is the LLM prevented from directly mutating state?
- Are outputs constrained by schema/contracts?
- Is there an append-only log or durable transaction record?
- Can state be replayed or reconstructed?
- Are task boundaries explicit?
- Are failures handled through hotfixes, issues, or compensations?
- Are agents isolated by role, permission, and scope?

### Relevant Papers

- **ESAA**: strongest architecture layer
- **SagaLLM**: strongest compensation/recovery layer
- **ESAA-Security**: applies architecture to security audits

### Core Finding

The best architecture combines:

- ESAA-style **event sourcing**
- SagaLLM-style **compensation**
- ESAA-Security-style **domain playbooks and evidence artifacts**

---

## 2. UX / Operator Audit

Evaluate whether humans can understand, trust, and act on the system.

### Checks

- Can the operator see what happened and why?
- Are findings traceable to evidence?
- Are risk scores understandable?
- Are remediation steps actionable?
- Are failures surfaced clearly?
- Can non-experts consume the executive summary?
- Can experts drill down into check-level evidence?

### Relevant Papers

- **ESAA-Security** is strongest here because it produces:
  - vulnerability inventories
  - severity classifications
  - risk matrices
  - remediation guidance
  - executive summaries
  - final Markdown/JSON reports

### Core Finding

A governed agent system is not enough. The operator needs a **clear evidence-to-decision interface**.

The final report should not be “LLM prose.”  
It should be a projection of structured evidence.

---

## 3. Live QA / Validation Audit

Evaluate whether the system actually works under execution.

### Checks

- Does replay verification pass?
- Do invalid outputs get rejected?
- Can the system recover from failed steps?
- Are compensations tested?
- Are final reports internally consistent with artifacts?
- Does the audit cover all declared domains/checks?
- Can a second run reproduce the same state?
- Are findings grounded in actual files, configs, or logs?

### Relevant Papers

- **ESAA**: replay/hash verification
- **SagaLLM**: compensation and recovery testing
- **ESAA-Security**: artifact completeness and audit coverage

### Core Finding

The key QA distinction:

> A system can be perfectly replayable and still produce weak conclusions.

So Live QA must test both:

1. **Governance correctness**
2. **Domain correctness**

---

# Deep Research Using the Pipeline  
## Architecture → UX → Live QA

Scope:

- [ESAA-Security — arXiv:2603.06365](https://arxiv.org/pdf/2603.06365)
- [ESAA — arXiv:2602.23193](https://arxiv.org/pdf/2602.23193)
- [SagaLLM — arXiv:2503.11951](https://arxiv.org/pdf/2503.11951)

---

# 1. Architecture Audit

## Verdict: **Strong / Promising**

All three papers converge on the same architectural thesis:

> LLM agents should not directly mutate trusted state. They should emit structured intentions that are validated, logged, projected, and verified by deterministic infrastructure.

## Architecture Findings

### A. State Governance

| Paper | State Model | Assessment |
|---|---|---|
| **ESAA** | Append-only event log + projected roadmap | Strongest state model |
| **ESAA-Security** | ESAA event model specialized for audit artifacts | Strong domain specialization |
| **SagaLLM** | Persistent transaction state + compensation metadata | Strong recovery model |

**Finding:**  
ESAA provides the cleanest source-of-truth model: the event log is authoritative, and current state is derived through replay.

### B. Mutation Boundary

All three papers correctly separate:

```mermaid
graph LR
    A[LLM Agent] --> B[Structured Intent]
    B --> C[Validator / Orchestrator]
    C --> D[State Mutation]
    D --> E[Replayable / Recoverable State]
```

This is the right architecture for governed agents.

### C. Validation Layer

- **ESAA** uses schema validation, contracts, event replay, and hashing.
- **ESAA-Security** adds domain-specific security checks and audit contracts.
- **SagaLLM** uses a GlobalValidationAgent plus transaction constraints.

**Risk:** SagaLLM’s validation agent may itself be LLM-based, so production use needs deterministic validators wherever possible.

### D. Recovery Model

| Paper | Recovery Strategy |
|---|---|
| **ESAA** | Preserve history; issue/hotfix paths rather than silent mutation |
| **ESAA-Security** | Reconstruct audit state and final report from admitted events |
| **SagaLLM** | Saga-style compensating transactions |

**Best combined model:**  
Use **ESAA for immutable traceability** and **SagaLLM for reversible external actions**.

## Architecture Risks

### P0 / Critical

None in concept.

### P1 / High

1. **Governed state does not guarantee correct domain output.**  
   A flawed security playbook can produce a perfectly replayable but incomplete audit.

2. **Validator trust is under-specified.**  
   LLM-based validators need deterministic backup checks.

3. **Compensation correctness is hard.**  
   SagaLLM assumes compensations can be generated and validated safely, but real-world rollback is often partial or irreversible.

### P2 / Medium

- More benchmark-scale validation is needed.
- Conflict resolution for concurrent file edits remains future work.
- ESAA-Security needs empirical comparison against human and tool-based AppSec audits.

---

# 2. UX / Operator Audit

## Verdict: **Partial / Needs Productization**

The papers are architecturally strong, but the operator experience is less mature.

## UX Findings

### A. Operator Visibility

ESAA and ESAA-Security provide strong raw materials:

- event logs
- roadmap state
- check results
- vulnerability inventories
- risk matrices
- final reports

But the papers do not fully define a polished operator interface.

**UX requirement:** Operators need to see:

```mermaid
graph LR
    A[Finding] --> B[Evidence]
    B --> C[Severity]
    C --> D[Remediation]
    D --> E[Verification Status]
```

### B. Evidence Traceability

**ESAA-Security is strongest here.**

Its best UX idea is that the final audit report is not free-form LLM prose. It is a projection of:

- check-level evidence
- domain findings
- severity classifications
- risk matrix
- remediation guidance
- executive summary

This is the right pattern.

### C. Executive Usability

ESAA-Security includes:

- 0–100 security score
- top risks
- executive summary
- remediation guidance

That is useful for leadership, but needs strong guardrails so the score does not imply false certification.

### D. Developer Usability

Developers need:

- file path
- vulnerable code/config reference
- exploit explanation
- fix recommendation
- severity rationale
- verification command/test

ESAA-Security implies this, but the paper does not yet prove the generated reports consistently meet that bar.

## UX Risks

### P1 / High

1. **Replayability may be invisible to operators.**  
   If the UI only shows final reports, users may miss the audit trail value.

2. **Risk scores can create false confidence.**  
   A 0–100 score must be clearly labeled as internal audit maturity, not certification.

3. **Too much event detail can overwhelm users.**  
   The UI needs layered disclosure: executive → technical → forensic.

### P2 / Medium

- Need report diffing between audit runs.
- Need “finding lifecycle” states: open, accepted risk, fixed, false positive, verified.
- Need clear failed-check and blocked-check treatment.

---

# 3. Live QA / Validation Audit

## Verdict: **Promising but Incomplete**

The live QA evidence is strongest for ESAA, weaker for ESAA-Security, and mixed for SagaLLM.

## Live QA Findings

### A. ESAA

Reported case studies:

| Case | Tasks | Events | Agents | Verification |
|---|---:|---:|---:|---|
| Landing page | 9 | 49 | 3-agent composition | `verify_status=ok` |
| Clinical dashboard | 50 | 86 | 4 concurrent agents | `verify_status=ok`, partial project |

**Strength:** Demonstrates replayable state and concurrent multi-agent orchestration.

**Limitation:** `verify_status=ok` proves projection integrity, not software quality.

### B. ESAA-Security

Defines the right QA dimensions:

- protocol compliance
- replay-verifiable state integrity
- coverage completeness
- artifact completeness
- risk-report usefulness

But the paper mostly presents an evaluation design, not a completed large empirical evaluation.

**Live QA status:** conceptually strong, empirically early.

### C. SagaLLM

Evaluates planning scenarios from the REALM benchmark and shows that standalone LLMs miss constraints in reactive planning.

**Strength:** Good demonstration of context loss and need for independent validation.

**Limitation:** Production-grade compensation and real external side effects are not deeply proven.

## Live QA Checklist

For a production implementation inspired by these papers, I would require:

```markdown
- Replay verification passes
- Invalid agent output is rejected
- Boundary violation is rejected
- Completed task cannot be silently reopened
- Compensation path is tested
- Security finding has concrete evidence
- Final report matches underlying artifacts
- Same event log reproduces same projected state
- Human reviewer can trace every conclusion
```

## Live QA Risks

### P1 / High

1. **Governance QA is not enough.**  
   Need domain QA: did it find real vulnerabilities, produce correct fixes, and avoid false positives?

2. **Compensation needs adversarial testing.**  
   Rollback logic must be tested under partial failure, API failure, timeout, and irreversible action scenarios.

3. **Security audit coverage must be benchmarked.**  
   ESAA-Security needs test repos with known vulnerabilities.

### P2 / Medium

- Need fuzzing of malformed agent outputs.
- Need replay under version migration.
- Need concurrent conflict simulation.
- Need report consistency checks.

---

# Final Verdict

## Overall Assessment: **Strong Architectural Direction, Early Empirical Maturity**

These papers are valuable because they shift agent reliability away from prompt craft and toward system architecture.

The strongest combined insight is:

> Reliable agent systems need evented state, constrained outputs, deterministic validation, replay verification, and compensation paths.

## Priority Findings

### P0

None.

### P1

1. **Add deterministic validators wherever possible.**
2. **Benchmark domain correctness, not just protocol correctness.**
3. **Combine event sourcing with compensation for real-world workflows.**
4. **Make evidence traceability visible in the operator UX.**

### P2

1. Add audit-run diffing.
2. Add finding lifecycle management.
3. Add known-vulnerability benchmark repos.
4. Add replay and compensation stress tests.

---

# Recommended Next Step

Use the combined model:

```mermaid
graph TD
    A[Agent Intent] --> B[Schema / Contract Validation]
    B --> C[Append-only Event Log]
    C --> D[Projected State]
    D --> E[Replay Verification]
    B --> F[Saga Compensation Layer]
    D --> G[Evidence Artifacts]
    G --> H[Risk / Decision Report]
```

**Best practical implementation path:**

1. Start with **ESAA-style event sourcing**.
2. Add **ESAA-Security-style evidence artifacts**.
3. Add **SagaLLM-style compensation** only where actions are externally consequential or reversible.

# Elephant Rock Research

**v0.1.0** ![status](https://img.shields.io/badge/status-alpha-orange)

**Elephant Rock** is an AI-powered research idea generation platform that automates the entire lifecycle of academic ideation — from literature discovery and gap analysis through novel idea generation, feasibility scoring, and structured proposal export. Feed it a research domain and it produces scored, cited research proposals with novelty and feasibility reports, ready for refinement.

---

## 30-Second Quick Start

```bash
# 1. Install (Python ≥ 3.11 required)
pip install -e ".[dev]"

# 2. Configure — interactive wizard validates your API key
erock setup

# 3. Run the dev environment (backend :8000 + frontend :3000)
erock dev

# 4. Generate your first research ideas
erock generate --domain "AI/NLP" --rounds 2 --ideas 3
```

> **Tip:** `erock setup` creates your `.env` file and optionally runs a test pipeline.
> Use `erock dev` to start both the FastAPI backend and React frontend with live reload.

---

## Architecture

Elephant Rock runs a **9-stage pipeline** that transforms raw literature into scored research proposals:

```
┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
│                     Elephant Rock 9-Stage Pipeline                   │
│                                                                      │
│  1. Literature Search ──► Discover papers from Semantic Scholar,     │
│                            arXiv, and OpenAlex                        │
│                          │                                           │
│  2. PDF Ingestion    ──► Parse, chunk, and index full-text PDFs      │
│                          │                                           │
│  3. Knowledge Base   ──► Embed chunks into ChromaDB + BM25 hybrid    │
│                            vector store with Knowledge Graph          │
│                          │                                           │
│  4. Gap Analysis     ──► Identify unsolved problems via multi-agent  │
│                            reasoning with clustering                  │
│                          │                                           │
│  5. Idea Generation  ──► Generate novel research ideas using a DAG   │
│                            of specialised agents (TopoAgent DAG)      │
│                          │                                           │
│  6. Novelty Check    ──► Score ideas against the knowledge base      │
│                            (method, problem, domain transfer)         │
│                          │                                           │
│  7. Feasibility      ──► Assess data, compute, and method viability  │
│     Scoring               with counterfactual analysis               │
│                          │                                           │
│  8. Proposal         ──► Synthesize structured proposals with        │
│     Synthesis             references and governance validation        │
│                          │                                           │
│  9. Export           ──► Output proposals to Markdown or LaTeX       │
│                                                                      │
└──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

   ┌─────────────────┐   ┌──────────────┐   ┌───────────────────┐
   │  Tiered Memory   │   │  Governance  │   │  Cost Router &    │
   │  (Semantic +     │   │  Validator   │   │  Budget Manager   │
   │   Episodic +     │   │  & Audit Log │   │  (token tracking) │
   │   Procedural)    │   │              │   │                   │
   └─────────────────┘   └──────────────┘   └───────────────────┘
```

### Key Design Principles

- **Multi-Agent Architecture**: Ideas are generated and critiqued by specialised agents coordinated via a DAG executor, with configurable topologies.
- **Hybrid Knowledge Base**: Semantic (ChromaDB) + lexical (BM25) retrieval with Reciprocal Rank Fusion.
- **Tiered Memory**: The platform retains lessons across runs via semantic, episodic, and procedural memory tiers.
- **Governance Layer**: All outputs pass through a configurable validator with audit logging for responsible research automation.

---

## Interfaces

### CLI (`erock`)

The CLI provides full access to every pipeline stage and utility:

| Command | Description |
|---|---|
| `erock setup` | Interactive setup wizard — configure provider, API key, and generate `.env` |
| `erock dev` | Start backend (port 8000) and frontend (port 3000) dev servers |
| `erock generate` | Run the full 9-stage pipeline |
| `erock search <query>` | Search academic literature across Semantic Scholar, arXiv, OpenAlex |
| `erock ingest <file>` | Ingest a PDF into the knowledge base |
| `erock novelty-check <text>` | Check novelty of a research idea |
| `erock feasibility-score <text>` | Score feasibility of a research idea |
| `erock autonomous` | Run autonomous research cycles |
| `erock ideas` | List stored research ideas |
| `erock gaps` | List identified research gaps |
| `erock runs` | List pipeline run history |
| `erock knowledge search <query>` | Search the knowledge base |
| `erock status` | Show system status and configuration |
| `erock config` | Display key configuration settings |

All commands accept `--debug` for verbose tracebacks.

### Web UI

Start with `erock dev` and open **http://localhost:3000**. The React frontend provides a visual interface for running pipelines, browsing ideas, and exploring the knowledge base.

### REST API

The backend exposes a FastAPI server at **http://localhost:8000** with full Swagger docs at **http://localhost:8000/docs**.

**Key endpoints** (all under `/api/v1`, authenticated via `EROCK_API_KEY` if set):

| Method | Endpoint | Description |
|---|---|---|
| `POST` | `/api/v1/pipeline/run` | Start a pipeline run |
| `GET` | `/api/v1/pipeline/runs` | List pipeline runs |
| `GET` | `/api/v1/pipeline/runs/detail/{id}` | Get run details |
| `POST` | `/api/v1/pipeline/resume/{id}` | Resume a paused run |
| `POST` | `/api/v1/pipeline/autonomous` | Start autonomous cycle |
| `GET` | `/api/v1/ideas` | List research ideas |
| `GET` | `/api/v1/ideas/{id}` | Get idea details |
| `POST` | `/api/v1/ideas/{id}/feedback` | Submit idea feedback |
| `POST` | `/api/v1/ideas/{id}/refine` | Refine an idea |
| `GET` | `/api/v1/gaps` | List research gaps |
| `GET` | `/api/v1/knowledge/stats` | Knowledge base statistics |
| `POST` | `/api/v1/knowledge/search` | Search the knowledge base |
| `GET` | `/api/v1/status` | System status |
| `GET` | `/health` | Health check (unauthenticated) |

> See the full interactive API reference at `http://localhost:8000/docs` when the server is running.

---

## Configuration

All settings are managed via environment variables with the `EROCK_` prefix. Copy the included template and add your keys:

```bash
cp .env.example .env
# Or use the guided wizard:
erock setup
```

**Essential variables** (see `.env.example` for the full list):

| Variable | Default | Description |
|---|---|---|
| `EROCK_DEFAULT_PROVIDER` | `openai` | LLM provider (`openai`, `anthropic`, `gemini`, `ollama`) |
| `EROCK_OPENAI_API_KEY` | — | OpenAI API key |
| `EROCK_ANTHROPIC_API_KEY` | — | Anthropic API key |
| `EROCK_GEMINI_API_KEY` | — | Google Gemini API key |
| `EROCK_DATABASE_URL` | `sqlite:///./data/elephant_rock.db` | Database connection string |
| `EROCK_CHROMA_PERSIST_DIR` | `./data/chroma` | Vector store directory |
| `EROCK_GENERATION_ROUNDS` | `2` | Number of idea generation rounds |
| `EROCK_IDEAS_PER_ROUND` | `3` | Ideas produced per round |

> **Important:** Never commit real API keys. Use placeholder format like `sk-your-key-here` in examples.

Full configuration reference: [`backend/config.py`](backend/config.py) · [`.env.example`](.env.example)

---

## Contributing

Contributions are welcome. To get started:

1. **Fork** the repository and create a feature branch.
2. **Install** with dev dependencies: `pip install -e ".[dev]"`
3. **Run tests**: `pytest` (baseline: 1,370 tests)
4. **Lint**: `ruff check backend/`
5. **Type-check**: `mypy backend/`
6. **Submit** a pull request with a clear description of the change.

### Project Structure

```
elephant-rock-platform/
├── backend/
│   ├── api/            # FastAPI routes and middleware
│   ├── cli/            # Typer CLI commands

│   │   └── export/        # Stage 9: export (Markdown/LaTeX)

  - gap_analysis:
      method: llm_cluster_analysis
      clustering: kmeans_with_auto_k
      min_gaps: 1
  - idea_generation:
      method: tree_search
      max_depth: 3
      branching: 4
      reflection: true
      max_iterations: 3
  - novelty_checking:
      method: embedding_similarity
      threshold: 0.85
  - feasibility_scoring:
      dimensions: [data_availability, method_complexity, computational_cost]
      scale: 0_to_1
  - proposal_synthesis:
      strategies: [fast_scan, deep_research, academic_proposal, literature_review]
      fast_scan_sections: 3
      deep_research_sections: 10+
  - evaluation:
      dimensions: [novelty, feasibility, completeness, rigor, clarity]
      scale: 0_to_1
  - knowledge_library:
      storage: sqlite
      dedup: sha256_title_hash
      types: [paper, gap, idea]
  - journal:
      formats: [notes_md, readme_md]
      scrub_sensitive: true
  - reflection:
      max_iterations: 3
      fail_open: true
  - soul:
      file: SOUL.md
      inject: system_prompt
constraints:
  - No API keys required for core functionality (graceful degradation)
  - All LLM calls respect provider rate limits
  - Embedding dimensions depend on provider (768 for Ollama nomic-embed-text)
  - Proposal length varies by strategy (fast: ~3K, deep: ~35K chars)
  - Pipeline requires at least 1 literature source to generate gaps
  - Knowledge library is per-domain SQLite — no cross-domain sharing
  - Journal entries scrub API keys and sensitive patterns
  - Reflection loop is fail-open — timeout returns original results
  - Relevance filter guarantees minimum 5 papers when available
integrations:
  llm_providers: [ollama, openai, anthropic, z.ai]
  embedding_providers: [ollama, openai]
  search_sources: [arxiv, openalex, semantic_scholar, pubmed, crossref]
  export_formats: [markdown, json, bibtex]

# Elephant Rock Research Platform

## Quick Start
```bash
# Start backend
cd backend && uvicorn backend.api.app:app --reload

# Start frontend
cd frontend && npm run dev
```

## Pipeline Stages (in order)
1. `literature_search` — Search across multiple academic sources
2. `ingestion` — Download and parse full-text papers
3. `gap_analysis` — Identify knowledge gaps via LLM cluster analysis
4. `idea_generation` — Generate novel ideas via tree search
5. `novelty_checking` — Score ideas against existing literature
6. `feasibility_scoring` — Evaluate practical implementability
7. `mechanical_metrics` — Compute objective quality metrics
8. `proposal_synthesis` — Generate complete research proposals
9. `export` — Output in multiple formats

## API Endpoints
- `POST /api/pipeline/runs` — Start a pipeline run
- `GET /api/pipeline/runs` — List all runs
- `GET /api/pipeline/runs/{id}` — Get run details
- `POST /api/search` — Search literature directly
- `GET /api/ideas` — List generated ideas
- `GET /api/gaps` — List identified gaps

# Architecture

Elephant Rock is built around a **9-stage pipeline** that transforms raw literature
into scored, cited research proposals.

---

## System Overview

```
┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
│                     Elephant Rock 9-Stage Pipeline                   │
│                                                                      │
│  1. Literature Search ──► Discover papers from Semantic Scholar,     │
│                            arXiv, and OpenAlex                        │
│                          │                                           │
│  2. Gap Detection     ──► Identify methodological, empirical, and    │
│                            theoretical gaps in the literature         │
│                          │                                           │
│  3. Idea Generation   ──► Generate novel research ideas targeting    │
│                            detected gaps                              │
│                          │                                           │
│  4. Novelty Check     ──► Verify ideas against existing literature   │
│                            to ensure originality                      │
│                          │                                           │
│  5. Feasibility Score ──► Assess practical feasibility of each idea  │
│                          │                                           │
│  6. Synthesis         ──► Combine top ideas into coherent proposals  │
│                          │                                           │
│  7. Evaluation        ──► Multi-dimensional scoring and ranking      │
│                          │                                           │
│  8. Reporting         ──► Generate structured reports and exports    │
│                          │                                           │
│  9. Memory Store      ──► Persist learnings for future runs          │
│                                                                      │
└──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘
```

---

## Technology Stack

| Layer | Technology | Purpose |
|:------|:-----------|:--------|
| API | FastAPI | REST API with OpenAPI docs |
| Database | SQLite (SQLAlchemy) | Data persistence |
| Vector Store | ChromaDB | Semantic search / embeddings |
| LLM | LiteLLM | Multi-provider LLM abstraction |
| Frontend | React | Web UI |
| Migrations | Alembic | Database schema versioning |
| Auth | JWT (python-jose) | Authentication & RBAC |
| Observability | Custom tracing | Distributed traces & metrics |

---

## Backend Architecture

### API Layer (`backend/api/`)

The API layer is built with FastAPI and organized into route modules:

```
backend/api/
├── app.py              # FastAPI application factory
├── auth.py             # JWT authentication & password hashing
├── errors.py           # Standardized error handling
├── schemas.py          # Pydantic request/response schemas
└── routes/
    ├── auth.py         # Registration, login, user management
    ├── collaboration.py # Comments and sharing
    ├── costs.py        # Cost tracking endpoints
    ├── exports.py      # PDF and ZIP export
    ├── gaps.py         # Research gap endpoints
    ├── governance.py   # Human-in-the-loop approvals
    ├── ideas.py        # Research idea CRUD
    ├── knowledge.py    # Knowledge base management
    ├── knowledge_graph.py # Entity-relationship graph
    ├── literature.py   # Literature search and ingest
    ├── memory.py       # Agent memory system
    ├── pipeline.py     # Pipeline orchestration & sessions
    ├── plugins.py      # Plugin management
    └── traces.py       # Observability endpoints
```

### Pipeline Layer (`backend/pipeline/`)

Each pipeline stage is a self-contained module:

```
backend/pipeline/
├── orchestrator.py     # Pipeline execution engine
├── literature/         # Stage 1: Literature search
├── gaps/               # Stage 2: Gap detection
├── generation/         # Stage 3: Idea generation
├── novelty/            # Stage 4: Novelty checking
├── feasibility/        # Stage 5: Feasibility scoring
├── synthesis/          # Stage 6: Proposal synthesis
├── evaluation/         # Stage 7: Multi-dimensional scoring
├── reporting/          # Stage 8: Report generation
├── memory/             # Stage 9: Memory persistence
├── knowledge/          # Knowledge graph & retrieval
├── governance/         # Approval workflow
└── observability/      # Tracing & metrics
```

### Provider Layer (`backend/providers/`)

The provider layer abstracts LLM access through LiteLLM:

```
backend/providers/
├── provider_factory.py # Provider registry & factory
├── routing/            # Cost-aware model routing
└── task_router.py      # Task-specific model selection
```

---

## Data Flow

### Pipeline Execution

```
CLI / API Request
       │
       ▼
┌──────────────┐
│ Orchestrator  │  Creates run, dispatches async task
└──────┬───────┘
       │
       ▼
┌──────────────┐
│ Stage Runner  │  Executes stages sequentially
└──────┬───────┘
       │
       ├──► Literature Search (Semantic Scholar, arXiv, OpenAlex)
       ├──► Gap Detection (LLM-powered analysis)
       ├──► Idea Generation (LLM-powered synthesis)
       ├──► Novelty Check (embedding similarity)
       ├──► Feasibility Scoring (multi-criteria assessment)
       ├──► Synthesis (proposal generation)
       ├──► Evaluation (scoring & ranking)
       ├──► Reporting (structured output)
       └──► Memory Store (persist learnings)
              │
              ▼
        Database / SSE Stream
```

### Authentication Flow

```
POST /api/v1/auth/register → Creates user, returns JWT
POST /api/v1/auth/login    → Validates credentials, returns JWT
GET  /api/v1/auth/me       → Returns current user (requires JWT)
```

JWT tokens are passed via the `Authorization: Bearer <token>` header.
API key auth is also supported via the `X-API-Key` header.

---

## Database Schema

The platform uses SQLAlchemy ORM with Alembic migrations. Key models:

| Model | Description |
|:------|:------------|
| `PipelineRun` | Tracks pipeline execution state and metadata |
| `Idea` | Generated research ideas with scores |
| `Gap` | Detected research gaps |
| `User` | User accounts with role-based access |
| `Comment` | Collaboration comments on ideas |
| `CostEvent` | Token usage and cost records |
| `MemoryEntry` | Persisted agent memories |

---

## Configuration

Settings are managed via `pydantic-settings` and can be configured through
environment variables or `.env` file:

```python
from backend.config import get_settings

settings = get_settings()
# settings.default_provider, settings.memory_enabled, etc.
```

See [Getting Started](getting-started.md) for the full list of configuration options.

# Pipeline Reliability Patterns from Reference Implementations

Research from Temporal, Airflow, Prefect, Dagster, Kestra, and Ray on handling
stuck tasks, heartbeat monitoring, state machines, silent failures, and checkpoint/resume.

---

## 1. Detecting & Handling Stuck/Running Tasks That Never Complete

### Airflow — Zombie Task Detection via Heartbeat Timeout
**File:** `airflow-core/src/airflow/jobs/scheduler_job_runner.py` (lines ~2870-3030)

Airflow's scheduler has a dedicated `_find_and_purge_task_instances_without_heartbeats` loop:
```python
def _find_task_instances_without_heartbeats(self, *, session: Session) -> list[TI]:
    limit_dttm = timezone.utcnow() - timedelta(seconds=self._task_instance_heartbeat_timeout_secs)
    task_instances_without_heartbeats = list(
        session.scalars(
            select(TI)
            .where(
                TI.state.in_((TaskInstanceState.RUNNING, TaskInstanceState.RESTARTING)),
                TI.last_heartbeat_at < limit_dttm,
            )
        )
    )
```
When found, it:
1. Logs a "heartbeat timeout" event
2. Sends a failure callback to the DAG processor
3. Changes state via `executor.change_state(ti.key, TaskInstanceState.FAILED, remove_running=True)`
4. Increments a `task_instances_without_heartbeats_killed` metric

### Airflow — Stuck-in-Queued Task Handling
**File:** `airflow-core/src/airflow/jobs/scheduler_job_runner.py` (lines ~2513-2630)

Tasks stuck in QUEUED state get requeued up to N times before being marked FAILED:
```python
def _handle_tasks_stuck_in_queued(self, session):
    tasks_stuck_in_queued = self._get_tis_stuck_in_queued(session)
    for executor, stuck_tis in self._executor_to_workloads(tasks_stuck_in_queued, session).items():
        for ti in stuck_tis:
            executor.revoke_task(ti=ti)
            self._maybe_requeue_stuck_ti(ti=ti, session=session, executor=executor)

def _maybe_requeue_stuck_ti(self, *, ti, session, executor):
    num_times_stuck = self._get_num_times_stuck_in_queued(ti, session)
    if num_times_stuck < self._num_stuck_queued_retries:
        self._reschedule_stuck_task(ti, session=session)
    else:
        ti.set_state(TaskInstanceState.FAILED, session=session)
        executor.fail(ti.key)
```

**Pattern:** Query for tasks in RUNNING/QUEUED that have exceeded a time threshold → revoke from executor → requeue or fail.

### Dagster — Orphaned Run Detection
**File:** `python_modules/dagster/dagster/_grpc/server.py` (lines ~540-580)

Dagster's gRPC server runs a periodic cleanup thread:
```python
def _check_for_orphaned_runs(self) -> None:
    with self._execution_lock:
        runs_to_clear = []
        for run_id, (process, instance_ref) in self._executions.items():
            if not process.is_alive():
                run = instance.get_run_by_id(run_id)
                if not run or run.is_finished:
                    continue
                message = get_run_crash_explanation(
                    prefix=f"Run execution process for {run.run_id}",
                    exit_code=process.exitcode,
                )
                instance.report_engine_event(message, run, cls=self.__class__)
                instance.report_run_failed(run)
        for run_id in runs_to_clear:
            self._clear_run(run_id)
```

**Pattern:** Periodically scan in-memory map of `{run_id → subprocess}` → check `process.is_alive()` → if dead + run not finished, mark as failed.

### Kestra — Stuck Execution Detection (Concurrency Limit)
**File:** `executor/src/main/java/io/kestra/executor/ConcurrencyLimitStateStore.java`

Kestra explicitly calls out preventing executions from getting "stuck in the queue indefinitely" (issue #13785), and in `DefaultExecutor.java` line 823:
```java
// that could leave executions stuck in the queue indefinitely (see issue #13785)
```

---

## 2. Heartbeat & Timeout Patterns for Long-Running Tasks

### Temporal — Activity Timeout Hierarchy
**File:** `api/matchingservice/v1/request_response.pb.go`

Temporal defines a 4-level timeout hierarchy for activities:
```
ScheduleToCloseTimeout   — total wall-clock time from task creation to completion
ScheduleToStartTimeout   — time waiting in queue before a worker picks it up
StartToCloseTimeout      — max execution time once a worker starts processing
HeartbeatTimeout         — max time between heartbeat pings during execution
```

**File:** `service/worker/scanner/history/scavenger.go`
```go
func (s *Scavenger) heartbeat(ctx context.Context) {
    // Heartbeat to prevent heartbeat timeout.
    s.heartbeat(ctx)
}
```

Activities must call `context.Heartbeat()` periodically. If `HeartbeatTimeout` elapses without a heartbeat, the activity is considered failed and can be retried. The SDK also supports `WorkflowTaskHeartbeatTimeout` for long-running workflow tasks:
```go
// File: service/history/configs/config.go
WorkflowTaskHeartbeatTimeout dynamicconfig.DurationPropertyFnWithNamespaceFilter
```

### Airflow — Task Instance Heartbeats
**File:** `airflow-core/src/airflow/jobs/job.py` (line ~100)

Jobs have a `latest_heartbeat` column:
```python
latest_heartbeat: Mapped[datetime | None] = mapped_column(UtcDateTime())
```

The scheduler loop periodically heartbeats all executors:
```python
# scheduler_job_runner.py ~line 1670
for executor in self.executors:
    executor.heartbeat()
```

The Go SDK worker (`go-sdk/pkg/worker/runner.go`) has a dedicated heartbeater:
```go
type heartbeater struct {
    heartbeatInterval time.Duration
}

func (h *heartbeater) Run(ctx context.Context, ...) {
    ticker := time.NewTicker(h.heartbeatInterval)
    defer ticker.Stop()
    for {
        select {
        case <-ctx.Done():
            return
        case <-ticker.C:
            err := h.heartbeat(ctx)
            if err != nil {
                // Task cancelled after too many failed heartbeats
            }
        }
    }
}
```

### Kestra — Service Liveness via Periodic Heartbeats
**File:** `core/src/main/java/io/kestra/core/server/ServiceLivenessManager.java`

Kestra's `ServiceLivenessManager` sends periodic state updates (heartbeats):
```java
@Override
protected void onSchedule(final Instant now) {
    serviceRegistry.all().stream()
        .filter(localServiceState -> localServiceState.isStateUpdatable().get())
        .forEach(localServiceState -> {
            ServiceInstance instance = updateServiceInstanceState(now, service, null, callback);
        });
}

@Override
protected Duration getScheduleInterval() {
    return serverConfig.liveness().heartbeatInterval();
}
```

Workers proactively self-disconnect if they fail to update their state before timeout:
```java
// Proactively disconnect a WORKER server when it fails to update its current state
// for more than the configured liveness timeout (this is to prevent zombie server).
if (isLivenessEnabled() && isWorkerServer() && isServerDisconnected(now)) {
    ServiceInstance updated = updateServiceInstanceState(
        now, service, Service.ServiceState.DISCONNECTED, ...
    );
    onStateTransitionFailureCallback.execute(now, service, updated, true);
}
```

### Ray — Replica Health Checks
**File:** `doc/source/serve/doc_code/fault_tolerance/replica_health_check.py`

Ray Serve deployments support configurable health checks:
```python
@serve.deployment(health_check_period_s=10, health_check_timeout_s=30)
class MyDeployment:
    def check_health(self):
        if not self._my_db_connection.is_connected():
            raise RuntimeError("uh-oh, DB connection is broken.")
```

**Pattern:** Periodically call `check_health()` on each replica → if it raises or times out, the replica is marked unhealthy and removed from the routing pool.

---

## 3. Run State Machine Patterns

### Temporal — Workflow Execution State Machine
**File:** `api/enums/v1/workflow.pb.go`
```go
type WorkflowExecutionState int32
const (
    WORKFLOW_EXECUTION_STATE_UNSPECIFIED = 0
    WORKFLOW_EXECUTION_STATE_CREATED     = 1
    WORKFLOW_EXECUTION_STATE_RUNNING     = 2
    WORKFLOW_EXECUTION_STATE_COMPLETED   = 3
    WORKFLOW_EXECUTION_STATE_ZOMBIE      = 4  // ← unique: explicit zombie state
    WORKFLOW_EXECUTION_STATE_VOID        = 5
    WORKFLOW_EXECUTION_STATE_CORRUPTED   = 6
)
```

Zombie workflows are those whose parent workflow completed but the child still has pending work. The system explicitly tracks this state to allow safe cleanup vs. forceful termination.

### Airflow — Task Instance States
**File:** `airflow-core/src/airflow/models/taskinstance.py` (implied from scheduler logic)
```
SCHEDULED → QUEUED → RUNNING → SUCCESS / FAILED
                   ↗ (deferred) DEFERRED → (reschedule) → SCHEDULED
```

DagRun states:
```
QUEUED → RUNNING → SUCCESS / FAILED
```

### Prefect — State Type Enum
**File:** `prefect-main/src/prefect/server/schemas/states.py`
```python
class StateType(AutoEnum):
    PENDING    = AutoEnum.auto()
    RUNNING    = AutoEnum.auto()

from backend.pipeline.self_improve.evolution import PipelineEvolver
from backend.pipeline.self_improve.frontier import ParetoFrontier
from backend.pipeline.self_improve.lessons import LessonExtractor
from backend.pipeline.stages import (
    AdversarialReviewStage,
    CitationAuditStage,
    ExportStage,
    FeasibilityScoringStage,
    GapAnalysisStage,
    IdeaGenerationStage,
    IngestionStage,
    LiteratureSearchStage,
    MechanicalMetricsStage,
    NoveltyCheckingStage,
    PaperSynthesisStage,
    PipelineStage,
    ProposalDeepeningStage,
    ProposalSynthesisStage,
    StageContext,
    TreeSearchStage,
)
from backend.pipeline.synthesis.proposal_synthesizer import ProposalSynthesizer

from backend.pipeline.verification.reference_verifier import ReferenceVerifier
from backend.providers.base import LLMProvider
from backend.providers.provider_factory import get_registry
from backend.providers.token_counter import TokenCounter
from backend.pipeline.compaction.middleware import CompactionMiddleware

logger = logging.getLogger(__name__)


class PipelineOrchestrator:
    """Coordinates the full research idea generation pipeline."""

    _STAGE_ORDER = [
        "literature_search",
        "ingestion",
        "gap_analysis",
        "gap_reflection",
        "idea_generation",
        "idea_reflection",
        "novelty_checking",
        "feasibility_scoring",
        "mechanical_metrics",
        "proposal_synthesis",
        "adversarial_review",
        "evaluation",
        "paper_synthesis",
        "citation_audit",
        "proposal_deepening",
        "export",
    ]

    def __init__(self, provider: LLMProvider | None = None, stage_callback=None, settings: "Settings | None" = None, strategy: str | None = None):
        settings = settings or get_settings()
        self._registry = get_registry()
        # Guard against Settings being passed as provider (positional arg confusion)
        if provider is not None and not hasattr(provider, "structured_output"):
            logger.warning(
                "PipelineOrchestrator received %s as 'provider'; ignoring and creating default",
                type(provider).__name__,
            )
            provider = None
        self._provider = provider or self._registry.create(settings=settings)
        self._cost_tracker = self._registry.cost_tracker
        self._stage_callback = stage_callback
        self._settings = settings

        # Hybrid model routing: local for thinking tasks, cloud for generation
        self._model_selector = None
        self._thinking_provider = None
        if getattr(settings, 'lmstudio_enabled', False) or getattr(settings, 'thinking_model', ''):
            try:
                from backend.pipeline.model_selection import ModelSelector
                self._model_selector = ModelSelector(settings)
                self._thinking_provider = self._model_selector.resolve('classify')
                logger.info(
                    "Hybrid model routing enabled: thinking=%s, generation=%s",
                    getattr(self._thinking_provider, 'provider_name', 'local'),
                    self._provider.provider_name if hasattr(self._provider, 'provider_name') else 'cloud',
                )
            except Exception as e:
                logger.warning("Model selector init failed, using single provider: %s", e)

        # Strategy: resolve config, default to deep_research (HB-02)
        from backend.pipeline.strategies import StrategyRegistry, register_presets
        self._strategy_registry = StrategyRegistry()
        register_presets(self._strategy_registry)
        self._strategy_name = strategy or "deep_research"
        self._strategy_config = self._strategy_registry.get(self._strategy_name)
        logger.info("Pipeline strategy: %s", self._strategy_name)

        # Task routing (optional per-stage model selection)
        self._task_router = None
        if getattr(settings, "model_routing_enabled", False) or getattr(settings, "cost_routing_enabled", False):

logger = logging.getLogger(__name__)


@contextmanager
def _override_provider(
    service: object, override: LLMProvider | None
) -> Generator[None, None, None]:
    """Temporarily swap a service's _provider with the override."""
    if not override or not hasattr(service, "_provider"):
        yield
        return
    saved = service._provider  # type: ignore[attr-defined]
    try:
        service._provider = override  # type: ignore[attr-defined]
        yield
    finally:
        service._provider = saved  # type: ignore[attr-defined]


@dataclass
class StageContext:
    """Shared mutable state passed between stages."""

    result: PipelineResult
    all_papers: list = field(default_factory=list)
    db_run_id: int | None = None
    params: dict = field(default_factory=dict)
    domain: str = "AI/NLP"
    run_id: str = ""
    search_queries: list[str] | None = None
    max_gaps: int = 5
    rounds: int = 2
    ideas_per: int = 3
    export_format: str | None = "markdown"
    provider_override: Any = None  # LLMProvider override for model routing
    journal: Any = None  # B162: Optional JournalWriter or callback


class PipelineStage(ABC):
    """Base class for pipeline stages."""

    @property
    @abstractmethod
    def name(self) -> str:
        ...

    @abstractmethod
    async def execute(self, ctx: StageContext) -> bool:
        """Execute the stage. Return False to halt the pipeline."""
        ...


class LiteratureSearchStage(PipelineStage):

    async def execute(self, ctx: StageContext) -> bool:

        pre_existing = []
        try:
            from backend.pipeline.knowledge.integration import KnowledgeIntegrationService
            service = KnowledgeIntegrationService()
            existing = service.query_existing_knowledge(ctx.domain)
            if existing.get("has_knowledge"):
                pre_existing = service._indexer.get_existing_papers(ctx.domain, limit=50)
                logger.info(
                    "Knowledge library: %d pre-existing papers for '%s'",
                    len(pre_existing), ctx.domain,
                )
            service.close()
        except Exception as e:
            logger.debug("Knowledge library query skipped: %s", e)

        # B160: Also retrieve locally uploaded documents from vector store
        local_docs = []

            from backend.config import get_settings
            from backend.pipeline.knowledge.embedding_service import EmbeddingService
            from backend.pipeline.knowledge.vector_store import VectorStore
            from backend.providers.provider_factory import create_provider

            settings = get_settings()
            provider = create_provider()
            embedding = EmbeddingService(provider)
            store = VectorStore(settings.chroma_persist_dir, embedding)

            results = await store.query(ctx.domain, n_results=20)

                    local_docs.append(r)

        except Exception as e:
            logger.debug("Local document retrieval skipped: %s", e)

        queries = ctx.search_queries or [
            f"{ctx.domain} recent advances",
            f"{ctx.domain} open problems",

        query_results = await asyncio.gather(
            *(self._search.search_all(q, limit_per_source=20) for q in queries),
            return_exceptions=True,
        )
        all_papers = []
        for query, result in zip(queries, query_results, strict=True):
            if isinstance(result, Exception):
                logger.warning("Query '%s' failed: %s", query[:50], result)
            else:
                all_papers.extend(result)
                logger.info("Found %d papers for query: %s", len(result), query)

        seen = set()

            key = p.doi if getattr(p, 'doi', None) else p.title.lower().strip()
            if key not in seen:
                seen.add(key)
                unique.append(p)

        fuzzy_unique = []
        for paper in unique:
            is_dup = any(
                SequenceMatcher(

                    paper.title.lower().strip(),
                    existing.title.lower().strip(),
                ).ratio() > 0.85
                for existing in fuzzy_unique
            )
            if not is_dup:
                fuzzy_unique.append(paper)
        if len(fuzzy_unique) < len(unique):
            logger.info(
                "Fuzzy dedup removed %d near-duplicates (%d → %d)",
                len(unique) - len(fuzzy_unique), len(unique), len(fuzzy_unique),
            )
        unique = fuzzy_unique

        if pre_existing:
            from backend.pipeline.literature.models import Paper, Author
            for entry in pre_existing:
                try:
                    content = json.loads(entry.get("content", "{}")) if isinstance(entry.get("content"), str) else entry.get("content", {})
                    paper = Paper(
                        id=f"lib:{entry.get('id', '')}",
                        source="knowledge_library",
                        title=entry.get("title", ""),
                        abstract=content.get("abstract", ""),
                        authors=[],
                        year=content.get("year"),
                        doi=content.get("doi"),
                    )
                    key = paper.doi if paper.doi else paper.title.lower().strip()
                    if key not in seen:
                        seen.add(key)
                        unique.append(paper)
                except Exception as e:
                    logger.debug("Failed to merge library paper: %s", e)
            logger.info("Merged %d papers from knowledge library", len([p for p in unique if getattr(p, 'source', '') == 'knowledge_library']))

        # B160: Merge locally uploaded documents
        if local_docs:
            from backend.pipeline.literature.models import Paper
            for doc in local_docs:
                meta = doc.get("metadata", {})

                    source="local_upload",
                    title=title,
                    abstract=content[:500] if content else "",
                    authors=[],
                )
                key = paper.title.lower().strip()
                if key not in seen:
                    seen.add(key)
                    unique.append(paper)
            logger.info(
                "Merged %d locally uploaded documents",
                len([p for p in unique if getattr(p, 'source', '') == 'local_upload']),

def _build_stages(self) -> list[PipelineStage]:
        ref_validator = ReferenceValidator(store=self._store)

        # Build the idea generation stage based on tree_of_thought_enabled flag (HB-01)
        idea_stage: PipelineStage
        if getattr(self._settings, "tree_of_thought_enabled", False):
            from backend.pipeline.generation.tree_search import TreeSearchConfig, TreeSearchEngine

            tree_config = TreeSearchConfig(
                beam_width=getattr(self._settings, "tree_of_thought_beam_width", 2),
                max_depth=getattr(self._settings, "tree_of_thought_max_depth", 3),
            )
            # Use the existing ideator agent (implements the Ideator protocol)
            tree_engine = TreeSearchEngine(
                ideator=self._agent,  # IdeatorAgent implements the Ideator protocol
                config=tree_config,
            )
            idea_stage = TreeSearchStage(
                engine=tree_engine,
                hooks=self._hooks,
                provider=self._provider,
                kg=self._kg,
            )
            logger.info(
                "TreeSearchStage enabled (beam_width=%d, max_depth=%d)",
                tree_config.beam_width, tree_config.max_depth,
            )
        else:
            idea_stage = IdeaGenerationStage(
                self._agent,
                self._hooks,
                dag_executor=self._dag_executor,
                dag_agents=self._dag_agents,
                provider=self._provider,
                kg=self._kg,
                forest=self._forest,
                reasoning_verifier=self._reasoning_verifier,
            )

        # Adversarial review stage — uses thinking provider (local) to review
        # proposals generated by the generation provider (cloud)
        from backend.providers.provider_factory import get_thinking_provider
        thinking_provider = self._thinking_provider
        if thinking_provider is None:
            try:
                thinking_provider = get_thinking_provider(self._settings)
            except Exception as e:
                logger.warning("Could not resolve thinking provider for adversarial review: %s", e)

        adversarial_stage = self._build_adversarial_review_stage(
            synthesizer=self._synthesizer,
            thinking_provider=thinking_provider,
        )

        return [
            LiteratureSearchStage(self._search, self._hooks),
            IngestionStage(self._store, self._bm25, self._embedding, kg=self._kg, provider=self._provider),
            GapAnalysisStage(self._gap_analyzer, self._goal_manager, self._hooks, self._memory, kg=self._kg, faithfulness_checker=self._faithfulness_checker),
            idea_stage,
            NoveltyCheckingStage(self._novelty, self._hooks),
            FeasibilityScoringStage(self._feasibility),
            MechanicalMetricsStage(),
            self._build_synthesis_stage(ref_validator),

            CitationAuditStage(provider=thinking_provider),

        generation_rounds: int | None = None,
        ideas_per_round: int | None = None,

        run_feasibility: bool = True,

        run_id: str | None = None,
        session_id: str | None = None,
        skip_stages: set[str] | None = None,

    try:

        structlog.get_logger().info(
            "request",
            method=request.method,
            path=request.url.path,
            status=response.status_code,
            elapsed_ms=round(elapsed * 1000, 2),

        content={

                "hint": "Check request body fields against the API schema",

        headers={"X-Request-Id": request_id},
    )
